translation: Every high honour here in the world is surrounded by dangers; just as worldly distinctions are greater, so the dangers are stronger. Thus we can recognize and understand the examples from this. The tree, then, which grows in the woodland so that it towers up above all the other trees and spreads itself out—when suddenly a storm arises, and the strong wind, then it is shaken and battered more violently than the rest of the forest. It is likewise also with the high cliffs and crags: when they tower far up above the rest of the earth, they then suddenly begin to fall and crash very violently to the earth. Likewise also with the high mountains and hills, which stand high above the whole world: nevertheless they suffer the punishment of their eminence, in that they are often chastised and afflicted by heavenly fire, and struck by flames. So the high powers here in the world collapse and fall and come to ruin, and the riches of this world turn to sorrow, and these earthly wonders come to nothing.
translation_notes: ār here is high dignity/honour, not grace or mercy.
The tree sentence has a left-dislocated topic with later resumptive hit. The English dash is a translation aid, not source punctuation.
brǣt hit is reflexive spreading itself; do not make the storm the actor.
The storms illustrate risk attached to height, then the text transfers the comparison to worldly power.
torr here probably means a crag according to Cook156note12, not the productive earlier tower sense.
wīte habban ðæs ealdordōmes: suffer punishment on account of their eminence; the following ðæt explains it.
The literal repeated collapse/fall is preserved though Cook calls feallað pleonastic.
mihta can be rendered powers or potentates; the personification is contextual, not a unique new referential identity.
